projects.title: Selected Work
projects.intro: Six products at different stages: launched work, a market test, an honest prototype, one non-commercial experiment, and a private startup that is not ready to be shared yet. Each one says what I actually did and what happened next.

laibi.title: Supermarket Laibi 2
laibi.summary: I built a supermarket ordering PWA that feels at home on a phone and gives the owner one place to run the catalog and orders.
laibi.contribution: Product structure, UX, full-stack development, PWA, and admin workflows.
laibi.result: First-month sales reached roughly 1.25 times their previous level, before any paid promotion.

images.cardAlt: Supermarket Laibi 2 web app project card

context.title: Online ordering without funding two native apps
context.body: The owner wanted a direct digital ordering channel, but a separate mobile build would have swallowed budget without solving a different problem.

build.title: One PWA for customers, one admin system for the store
build.body: I handled the product structure, catalog, cart, installable mobile experience, order flow, and the admin tools for products, stock, categories, images, and orders.

outcome.title: A 1.25x first month without a paid campaign
outcome.body: First-month sales reached roughly 1.25 times their previous level. Because the product is a PWA, the owner also avoided paying for a separate native app.

said.title: Said
said.summary: I designed and built a heavy-truck-parts storefront around exact references, brands, and stock, not just product photos.
said.contribution: Product structure, mobile UX, search and catalog flows, and a full-stack prototype.
said.result: It still uses mock data, so I am not presenting a launch or sales result yet.

images.cardAlt: Said heavy truck parts store project preview
images.mobileAlt: Said mobile shopping experience for heavy truck parts

context.title: A part that looks right can still be wrong
context.body: Truck-parts buyers need the exact reference, brand, weight, availability, and delivery details before they can trust a listing.

build.title: A catalog that puts identification before decoration
build.body: I shaped the search, categories, brands, saved products, cart, order tracking, and admin flow around the information buyers actually check.

outcome.title: Ready for real inventory, without a made-up result
outcome.body: The product is functional and browsable, but it has not entered day-to-day business use. This case study stops at what I actually built.

rimoochat.title: Rimoochat
rimoochat.summary: I built Rimoochat for my mother's handmade clothing business, with a simple path from seeing a piece to starting the right conversation.
rimoochat.contribution: Frontend development, mobile UX, product presentation, and the customer contact flow.
rimoochat.result: It became the business's main customer channel and cut repeated back-and-forth for both sides.

context.title: My mother's work needed one clear home online
context.body: Customers were arriving through scattered messages. They needed a place to see the work first, understand what was available, and get in touch with better context.

build.title: A storefront that leads into a useful conversation
build.body: I focused the product presentation and mobile flow around handmade clothing, then made the contact path clear enough to reduce repeated questions.

outcome.title: Less time lost on both sides
outcome.body: The website is now the main place customers discover the business and make contact. It also gives my mother a clearer way to manage those conversations.

unimarket.title: Unimarket
unimarket.summary: I built Unimarket as social commerce: the familiar rhythm of social media, but the feed is made of products and stores.
unimarket.contribution: Product architecture, UX, full-stack development, and the seller and buyer flows.
unimarket.result: The production MVP took one month and is now being tested in the market.

context.title: Social discovery built around products, not posts
context.body: The client wanted stores and buyers to meet through a familiar feed instead of another rigid catalog or classified-ads page.

build.title: A production MVP in one month
build.body: I built the product structure, authentication, store and buyer flows, product discovery, moderation, and the working foundation needed for a real market test.

outcome.title: A first version the client was happy to test
outcome.body: The client was satisfied with the result and the product is now testing its place in the market rather than pretending the idea is already proven.

roadmap.title: Auctions, product reels, and delivery connections
roadmap.body: Live auctions, short product videos, and delivery-agency integrations are on the roadmap. They are planned features, not shipped claims.

duks.title: DUKS Perfume
duks.summary: I designed and built DUKS as a playful Arabic-first perfume experience, using motion and responsive art direction to make one product feel like a campaign.
duks.contribution: Concept, visual direction, Arabic-first UX, responsive frontend, and interaction design.
duks.result: A finished personal experiment in cinematic product storytelling, not a commercial client launch.

images.cardAlt: DUKS perfume experimental website project card
images.mobileAlt: Arabic-first DUKS perfume experience on mobile

context.title: A playground for one product, not another catalog
context.body: I wanted to see how far one perfume could carry an entire experience when the page was treated like a campaign instead of an ordinary storefront.

build.title: Arabic-first art direction across desktop and mobile
build.body: I built the responsive layout, oversized Arabic type, product transitions, social and contact paths, and separate compositions for wide and narrow screens.

outcome.title: A finished experiment, with no commercial claim
outcome.body: DUKS is a personal fun project. It was not commissioned, and I am not attaching sales or client results to it. Its value is the visual and frontend exploration.

reperto.title: Reperto
reperto.summary: Reperto is complete. I built it as technical co-founder and co-owner, but the product itself stays private for now.
reperto.contribution: Technical co-founding, product architecture, full-stack implementation, and technical ownership.
reperto.result: The system is complete; I will share the case study and link after its intellectual-property protection is in place.

images.mobileAlt: Orange Reperto startup logo in a portrait composition

context.title: The product is finished; the public reveal comes later
context.body: We are keeping the product and its operating details private until the necessary intellectual-property protection is secured.

build.title: Technical co-founder and co-owner
build.body: I own the technical side, from product architecture and technical decisions through implementation and delivery.

outcome.title: Complete, with protection before publication
outcome.body: The system is done. I will publish the case study and startup link when we can share them without exposing what needs protection.

howIWork.title: How I take a project from rough idea to build.
howIWork.body: Discovery, scope, investment, and responsibilities get clear before development starts.

about.title: The person behind the build.
about.body: A little more about my engineering background, product thinking, and the kind of work I care about.

howIWork.title: How I work
howIWork.intro: A useful project starts with the business case: who needs it, what should become easier, where the value is, and what counts as a win.

discovery.label: Discovery call
discovery.value: Project context, target users, current workflow, risks, and success metrics get mapped first.

mvp.label: MVP shape
mvp.value: The first working version is defined clearly. Nice-to-have features wait.

agreement.label: Agreement
agreement.value: Scope, investment, timeline, milestones, and responsibilities are written before build starts.

chat.clientStart: Hey Heithem. I want to launch a store, startup, or web app. What should be clear before we start?
chat.heithemIntro: Happy to help. Send the rough version first: what the product should do, who will use it, and where it should make money or save time.
chat.heithemCall: A free 30-minute voice or video call is usually enough to map the idea, the risks, the first version, and the success metric.
chat.clientInvestment: Good. What kind of investment should I expect for the web app?
chat.heithemInvestment: The investment becomes clear after discovery. It depends on scope, complexity, timeline, integrations, and what the first version needs to prove.
chat.heithemRange: For a working online store with the important parts included, investment usually starts around $1.5k to $3k. Complex platforms need discovery first, then a clean number.
chat.clientCall: Makes sense. Let’s start with the call.
chat.callNote: Discovery call: project goal, users, MVP scope, risks, timeline, and success metrics.
chat.heithemAgreement: Next comes a short agreement: scope, investment, timeline, milestones, what is included, and what is needed from your side.
chat.heithemClose: Perfect. Once you give the OK on the agreement, work starts.

about.title: Web apps that move the business.

paragraphs.one: Specialized in building web apps using software engineering knowledge, turning complex business problems into clean, functional systems.
paragraphs.two: The work fits stores, startups, dashboards, and platforms where the app needs to handle real logic, not only look good on the first screen.
paragraphs.three: The goal is simple: create a product that helps sell, manage, decide, or save time through something people can use every day.

about.centerBody: Working for 2 startups as their tech co-founder and decision maker on the tech side of the work.

one.title: Experience aimed at business value.
one.text: With 5 years in engineering and 2 years developing web apps for startups and business owners, the focus is on targeted products designed to bring value to the investor based on the project’s real needs.

two.title: The client’s field becomes part of the app.
two.text: The best web apps feel specific. The client’s experience in the field becomes part of the product, then gets shaped into clean UI, strong speed, secure logic, and a web app that brings more value to the table.
